catalog_quote: In normal intonation (the affirmative of Voorhis) the primary stress and highest pitch fall on the second or the fourth syllable from the end of the word, the penult or the pre-antepenult. Pre-antepenultimate stress cannot be common in the world's languages, but as the final vowel in such words is devoiced perhaps the stress could be described as falling on the first or third from the end, counting only the stressable syllables. This devoicing is not found, however, in the word-final vowel sequences of the casual-style (5). Isolated words, as in one-word utterances or in lists, have the stress on the penult, as do words that have only two or three syllables: (7) nešakwe·némo̥ 'I was unwilling.' new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (25 pp., Adobe Paper Capture text layer; companion). Rendered PDF page 4 = printed p. 160 and read the page image: heading "E. Prosodic Features"; the quoted sentences are there word for word ("In normal intonation (the affirmative of Voorhis) the primary stress and highest pitch fall on the second or the fourth syllable from the end of the word, the penult or the pre-antepenult.. as the final vowel in such words is devoiced perhaps the stress could be described as falling on the first or third from the end, counting only the stressable syllables.. Isolated words, as in one-word utterances or in lists, have the stress on the penult, as do words that have only two or three syllables..…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (with highest pitch) is counted from the right edge and depends on utterance position: in citation/isolated forms and in all two- and three-syllable words it falls on the penult; longer words inside ordinary sentences typically carry it on the pre-antepenult (fourth from the end). Because the word-final short vowel is devoiced, Goddard notes this is equivalently 'first or third from the end counting only stressable syllables'. Under interrogative (yes-no) intonation the stress moves to the antepenult with raised pitch; the exclamative stresses and lengthens the final vowel. A host plus enclitic(s) is accented on the vowel immediately preceding the (last) enclitic (p. 163, 166).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with grave accent; 'One sometimes hears unexpected primary or secondary penultimate stress' (p. 160); the exclamative has a secondary stress on the pre-antepenult (p. 161).
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogative, exclamative, vocative, emphatic and interjectional intonations each place stress differently (antepenult; final vowel; penult; penult or pre-antepenult); some interjections have lexically inherent final accent; enclitic strings shift the accent to the syllable before the enclitic; compound stems are accented like ordinary words (pp. 160-166).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level in citation (penult) but sentence-level in running speech (pre-antepenult); stress and pitch are described together as intonation patterns, and Goddard leaves open whether all are contrastive. Data from 1990 fieldwork at Tama, Iowa (speakers Adeline Wanatee, Leonard Young Bear); the author calls the observations preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard 1991 describes Meskwaki proper as spoken at the Mesquakie Settlement, Tama, Iowa (1990 fieldwork), i.e. mesk1242; Sauk (Whittaker 2005, examined) is a separate Glottolog languoid and is not the basis of the statement. Jones 1911 is the same Fox variety (Tama) recorded a century earlier.

sources.note: §6 Stress (pp. 747-748): 'It is not possible to lay down definite rules for the determination of stress in every instance.. Generally, in words of two syllables, stress-accent falls on the first.; for words of three syllables, stress falls on the antepenult.. Beyond words of three syllables, only the semblance of a rule can be suggested. The chief stress comes on the first or second of the initial syllables, and the secondary stress on the penult'; §7 Pitch (p. 748): 'This Algonquian dialect does not fall wholly in the category of a stressed language. Pitch is ever present'. Older, impression…
